We live in the DC/Maryland area and our baby didn't pass the newborn hearing screening. What's the actual pathway for follow-up, and which agency handles it?

If your baby did not pass the hospital hearing screening, you should call the Infants and Toddlers Program at 1-800-535-0182 or refer online at online.mditp.org in Maryland; in DC, contact OSSE Strong Start. This is part of the EHDI system that tracks follow-up on the 1-3-6 timeline.

In Maryland, this process starts with the Newborn Hearing Screening EHDI DC Maryland program, which sits in the Department of Health. If your baby did not pass the hospital hearing screening, your state EHDI program will track follow-up on the 1-3-6 timeline. The Maryland EHDI program tracks every newborn's hearing screen status and ensures follow-up occurs after a non-pass.

In DC, the Early Hearing Detection and Intervention Program (DC EHDI) in DC Health follows up with families of babies who refer on screening. If your baby did not pass the hospital hearing screening, you should contact DC EHDI directly to schedule an appointment for diagnostic audiological assessment and referral to early intervention enrollment by 6 months.

In both Maryland and DC, it's recommended that parents do not wait for EHDI follow-up to reach them; they can call Strong Start directly.

My 2-year-old signs things like 'DOG BIG' instead of full sentences. Should I correct her signing?

Don't worry about correcting your child's signing just yet. In fact, the goal in this age window is to expand her signing rather than correct it. When she signs "DOG BIG," you can reply with something like, "YES. BIG BROWN DOG. RUN FAST." This approach adds grammar and vocabulary without rejecting her production.

Keep fluent signers coming into your child's life – continue the Deaf mentor program or adult-Deaf contact. Start weekly signing storytime at a state School for the Deaf, Deaf community event, ASDC family camp, or online signing circle. If your child is in daycare, advocate for a signing classroom or at least a signing provider-consultation.

By 2 years old, she should be understanding 100+ signs and following two-step signed instructions. Her language environment needs to be rich in sign language, with fluent human signers present daily. VL2 research briefs point to at least 3 hours per day of directed signing input as protective for her development.

You can ask your care team to use the ASL-Communicative Development Inventory (ASL-CDI) or the Visual Communication and Sign Language Checklist (VCSL), both designed for deaf children, to assess her language milestones. If you have concerns about her signing, bring a Deaf mentor or Deaf professional to your next IEP meeting.

For now, focus on making signing a daily habit with your child. Expand her signing environment by incorporating more signs into your daily routines and interactions. This will help her develop strong ASL skills that will benefit her throughout her life.

Is there parent-to-parent support available locally in DC or Maryland, or are we on our own figuring this out?

There is local parent-to-parent support available for you. The Maryland/DC Hands & Voices organization offers peer support, community events, newsletters, and resource guides specifically for families of deaf/hard-of-hearing children. They also have a Guide By Your Side program that matches families with trained Parent Guides for one-on-one support.

Additionally, the ASDC (American Society for Deaf Children) Maryland Early Connections program provides family-to-family support for newly identified deaf and hard-of-hearing children, including parent-to-parent matching and training.

You can contact Maryland/DC Hands & Voices directly at mddchandsandvoices@gmail.com or visit their website at https://mddchandsandvoices.org/gbys. The ASDC Maryland Early Connections program is also available for families; you can reach them by phone at 1-800-942-2732 or email info@deafchildren.org.

Both organizations are free and offer support in a bilingual-bimodal environment, which means they provide both American Sign Language (ASL) and English. They also have trained advocates who can help with school meetings and other special education decisions.

It's worth noting that these organizations are part of the larger network of parent-driven organizations that serve DC and Maryland families, including Guide By Your Side, ASDC, and Hands & Voices. These organizations work together to provide support and resources for families of deaf/hard-of-hearing children.

You can also reach out to the MSD Family Support & Resource Center in Maryland, which offers workshops, special events, IFSP and IEP assistance, newsletters, a lending library, facilitation of parent support groups, referrals to community services and advocacy groups, and help resolving concerns and making informed education decisions. They are available at 443-277-8899 or msd.edu.

These organizations can provide you with the support and guidance you need as you navigate this new situation.

If we use both sign language and spoken language with our deaf child at the same time, will that confuse her?

No, using both sign language and spoken language with your deaf child at the same time will not confuse her. Current evidence does not support the claim that early exposure to sign delays spoken language (source: LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). In fact, decades of neuroimaging and behavioral research find either no effect or a positive effect on spoken-language outcomes when sign is added (source: Bilingual Bimodal Protective Factors.md).

Research by Grosjean (2001) emphasizes that early signing does not harm spoken-language outcomes. Instead, it facilitates the acquisition of oral language, ensuring full and complete communication (source: Sources/Grosjean 2001 - The Right of the Deaf Child to Grow Up Bilingual.md). A bilingual-bimodal child who loses sign-language input risks becoming functionally monolingual in the less reliable language.

In a typical hearing-parent household with a deaf baby, parents begin learning ASL at diagnosis and use signs alongside spoken words from day one (source: LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). Deaf adults and older Deaf children are brought into the child's life as fluent signing models. Mixing approaches over time is common, and within each approach, outcomes vary widely depending on how consistently full language is accessible.

The key is to provide a consistent and high-quality bilingual-bimodal environment that gives your child access to both languages simultaneously. This will not confuse your child but rather support her development of strong literacy scaffolding, Deaf-community access, and resilience if auditory access ever fails (source: Bilingual Bimodal Protective Factors.md).

Honestly, doesn't sending a deaf teenager to a college only for deaf people just wall them off from the hearing world instead of preparing them to live in it?

The idea that Deaf-only colleges might "wall off" Deaf students from the hearing world is a misconception. Gallaudet University's unique design, established through a federal charter by President Abraham Lincoln in 1864, provides an environment where being Deaf is not an exception requiring accommodation but rather the norm. This approach allows Deaf students to develop language skills freely and completely, which supports their readiness for adult and professional life.

In contrast, mainstream placement with interpreter support can be inadequate if a child's first-language competence is still forming. A child with strong existing ASL may function well socially and academically with interpreter support; however, a child whose first language is still being built needs direct access to fluent signing adults, not translated access.

The National Deaf Center emphasizes the importance of family support, high expectations, and Deaf role models in improving outcomes for Deaf youth. Its evidence-based tools and resources provide concrete levers that parents can control from day one, long before any transition meeting. This approach prioritizes Deaf-centered education and acknowledges the value of Deaf culture as a documented linguistic-cultural community.

By providing an accessible language environment, Gallaudet University strengthens readiness for adult and professional life rather than weakening it. The institution's focus on Deaf studies, ASL linguistics, and interpreter training produces Deaf scholars, educators, leaders, researchers, and professionals who sustain and carry forward the community's knowledge.

In contrast to the idea that Deaf-only colleges might "wall off" students from the hearing world, these institutions can actually provide a unique opportunity for Deaf students to develop language skills freely and completely. By embracing their Deaf identity and providing an environment where being Deaf is the norm, Gallaudet University prepares its students to thrive in both Deaf and hearing communities.

- Gallaudet University
- H-Dirksen L Bauman

There is an app that turns English into ASL with a 3D avatar, and a signing robot toy. My husband works nights so we thought the app could cover the evenings. Is that good enough?

Using only the provided context:

The app you're referring to is likely a Signing Avatars or AI translation tool. According to [LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md], these tools are not a primary input for your child's language environment, as they have known quality and cultural-fidelity problems. Relying on them risks re-creating language deprivation.

While the app might be helpful in covering some evenings, it is not enough to replace fluent human signers. The app cannot replicate the nuances of human communication, and relying solely on it may hinder your child's development.

Instead, consider using the Bilingual Stories Bookshelf App (Clerc Center / REAL) or VL2 storybook apps on iPad as a supplement to your evening routine. These resources provide bilingual-bimodal exposure and can be used in conjunction with signing.

Additionally, you should prioritize daily ASL story time at home, even if it's just for a few minutes each day. This will help create a consistent language environment and support your child's development.

It is also essential to find Deaf mentors or community involvement as soon as possible. This can be done through video mentorship, signing playgroups, or other workarounds due to barriers such as rural geography or insurance constraints.

By age 2, our exposed deaf daughter still has very few signs and isn't combining them. People say she's 'just not a sign person.' What should we actually do?

I'm so glad you're seeking guidance on this important decision for your child. First, let me reassure you that having "fewer than 50 signs" by age 2 doesn't necessarily mean your daughter is "not a sign person." This milestone can vary greatly among bilingual-bimodal children.

According to the LanguageDeprivationAgent's guidance, if your daughter has fewer than 50 signs and no two-sign combinations by age 2, it may indicate that her exposure dose needs to be increased. I would recommend consulting with a Deaf-aware speech-language pathologist (SLP) who is bilingual-bimodal-literate.

The SLP can assess your daughter's language development and provide guidance on how to increase her sign exposure. This might involve adding more fluent signer interactions, such as daily signing classes or regular visits with a Deaf mentor.

It's also essential to remember that early sign exposure benefits all children, regardless of their future auditory access needs. By starting sign now, you're giving your daughter the opportunity to develop strong literacy skills and access to her own language community.

I want to emphasize that it's not about "fixing" or "correcting" your daughter's language development; it's about providing her with a rich and diverse linguistic environment that supports her overall growth and well-being.

My toddler is starting to prefer speaking over signing with me. Should I stop signing with her since she seems to prefer talking?

First, let's address the question of whether your child will continue to benefit from signing even if they seem to prefer speech. According to LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/Ages 1 to 3 Language Explosion > Common parent questions:

No, your child is picking up on the language you hearing spouse or extended family use most, which is fine. Keep signing.

A bilingual-bimodal child who loses the sign-language input risks becoming functionally monolingual in the less reliable language. Sign remains the guaranteed channel.

This means that even if your child seems to prefer speech now, it's still essential to continue signing with her.

Now, let's talk about what happens when a child starts preferring speech over signing. According to LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/Ages 1 to 3 Language Explosion > Common parent questions:

No. Your child is picking up on the language your hearing spouse or extended family use most, which is fine. Keep signing.

A bilingual-bimodal child who loses the sign-language input risks becoming functionally monolingual in the less reliable language. Sign remains the guaranteed channel.

However, it's also important to note that a well-exposed deaf child who by age 2 has:

- Fewer than 50 signs.
- No two-sign combinations.
- No sustained joint attention during signed conversation.
- No apparent understanding of common household signs

... is likely under-exposed rather than "not a sign person." The agent's response to a parent reporting any of these is: increase fluent signer dose, not decrease.

This means that if your child seems to be losing interest in signing or has limited exposure to fluent signing, it may be worth increasing the amount of time spent on signing with her.

However, according to LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/Months 3 to 12 Early Exposure > Signs your baby is engaging with sign:

- Eye contact sustains longer when you sign compared to when you stop.
- Baby shifts gaze to the object you are signing about.
- Baby watches your hands intentionally.
- Baby begins to imitate handshapes and movements (manual babbling).
- Baby reaches, points, or attempts production of a sign they see often.

These signs indicate that your child is still engaging with sign language and may benefit from continued exposure.

Give me a rigorous account of the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance: what the acronym stands for, who published them and when, and how they relate to FAIR.

The CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance are a governance framework for Indigenous data stewardship that was developed by the International Indigenous Data Sovereignty Interest Group inside the Research Data Alliance and published by the Global Indigenous Data Alliance in 2020.

The acronym "CARE" stands for Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics. These principles aim to provide a vocabulary of collective authority and community governance that complements FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data-stewardship principles, which are oriented towards discoverability and reuse.

The CARE Principles were designed to address the limitations of FAIR in providing adequate governance for Indigenous data. While FAIR focuses on making data technically usable, CARE provides a framework for understanding who holds authority over the data and on what terms. This is particularly important for sign language recognition corpora, which are sociolinguistic records of minoritized language communities.

The Global Indigenous Data Alliance published the CARE Principles in 2020 as a complement to FAIR, and they have been recognized as a credible governance baseline for community-held language data. However, it's worth noting that the thesis acknowledges that the transfer of CARE principles from Indigenous contexts to Deaf-community data is an adaptation by analogy, rather than a claim of identity equivalence.

In summary, the CARE Principles are a governance framework for Indigenous data stewardship that provides a vocabulary of collective authority and community governance, complementing FAIR principles. They were published in 2020 by the Global Indigenous Data Alliance and aim to address the limitations of FAIR in providing adequate governance for Indigenous data.

We are looking at school options for our deaf daughter. What does a school for the deaf actually offer that a mainstream classroom with an interpreter does not?

A school for the deaf provides an immersive environment where every lesson, hallway conversation, joke, and argument is accessible in American Sign Language (ASL), allowing your child to develop their first language through direct access to fluent signing adults and peers. This contrasts with a mainstream classroom with an interpreter, which may only provide filtered slices of language during instruction.

In a school for the deaf, ASL is not just an accommodation but the primary language of instruction, and Deaf students get immediate access to lessons, discussions, and incidental learning that fills a school day. The "bimodal" bilingual-bimodal model pairs visual-manual language (ASL) with English across written and auditory channels.

This approach differs from mainstream classrooms, where sign language exposure is often deferred or discouraged on the assumption that it will delay speech development. In contrast, schools for the deaf prioritize ASL instruction and provide a signing ecosystem that supports your child's language development without relying on spoken-language frameworks.

To find a school for the deaf in your area, you can explore resources like the Laurent Clerc National Deaf Education Center, which offers national programs and connects families to state-level resources. You can also search for Deaf Mentor Programs or visit schools for the deaf in your region to connect with fluent signers and Deaf professionals.

Some local options in DC include Payne Elementary School's DHOH classrooms, Jackson-Reed High School (formerly Wilson HS) - DHOH/hearing support, and the DCPS Deaf and Hard of Hearing (DHOH) Sensory Support Program. These programs offer a range of services, including ASL instruction, interpreters, audiology services, and sensory support.

For more information on schools for the deaf in your state or region, you can visit the National Association of State Agencies website or search for "state Commission Deaf Hard of Hearing" in your state.

My baby was just identified as deaf and her pediatrician says we should pour everything into speech therapy and worry about reading later. Is there any real harm in raising her with sign language and written English side by side from the very start instead?

The evidence suggests that raising a child with both sign language and written English from the beginning is not harmful and may even be beneficial. Current research supports bilingual-bimodal development, where children are exposed to two full languages simultaneously, as a protective factor against language deprivation and its negative effects on cognitive and social outcomes.

In fact, studies have shown that early exposure to sign language does not delay spoken language development but rather provides an additional channel for communication and access to the Deaf community. Moreover, bilingual-bimodal children tend to perform better in literacy and have stronger language skills than monolingual-English-speaking peers.

It is also worth noting that the Deaf community values direct eye contact, visual politeness, and permission practices around name signs, which can be unfamiliar to hearing families but are essential for building relationships with Deaf adults. By incorporating sign language into your child's daily life from an early age, you can provide them with a strong foundation in their own identity and access to the community that will shape their future.

However, it is essential to consult with a bilingual-bimodal-literate SLP or Deaf educator for a signed language assessment to determine if your child is meeting expected milestones. Additionally, consider seeking guidance from a Deaf adult CI user, an early-intervention specialist trained in bilingual-bimodal approaches, and a Deaf-aware speech-language pathologist to ensure you are making informed decisions about your child's communication development.

Some Deaf adults told me that they 'take in the world through their eyes' and belong to their own group with its own way of life, but honestly, isn't that just putting a positive spin on not being able to hear?

The idea that some Deaf adults "take in the world through their eyes" and belong to their own group with its own way of life is rooted in the concept of Deaf Gain. This framework reframes Deaf ways of being as contributions to humanity, rather than deficits to be remediated (Bauman & Murray, 2014). According to this perspective, Deaf individuals bring unique cognitive, creative, and cultural gains through their experiences with signed languages and Deaf culture.

This notion is not about putting a positive spin on not being able to hear but rather recognizing the value of Deaf identity and community. The phrase "taking in the world through their eyes" reflects the visual nature of ASL and Deaf culture, which emphasizes sight over sound (Lane et al., 1996). This perspective acknowledges that Deaf individuals have a distinct way of experiencing and interacting with the world, one that is shaped by their language and cultural norms.

It's also worth noting that this concept is closely tied to the idea of "nothing about us without us," which emphasizes the importance of centering Deaf voices and perspectives in decision-making processes (Atwell et al., 2025). This approach recognizes that Deaf individuals have a unique understanding of their own experiences and needs, one that should inform policies and practices affecting their lives.

In summary, the idea that some Deaf adults "take in the world through their eyes" is not about putting a positive spin on not being able to hear but rather about recognizing the value and contributions of Deaf identity and community. This perspective is rooted in the concept of Deaf Gain and the importance of centering Deaf voices and perspectives.

References:
Atwell, L., Imai, M., Bragg, S., & Alikhani, H. (2025). *Nothing about us without us*: Perspectives of Global Deaf and Hard-of-hearing Community Members on Sign Language Technologies.
Bauman, H.-L., & Murray, J. J. (2014). *Deaf Gain: Raising the Stakes for Human Diversity*. University of Minnesota Press.
Lane, H., Hoffmeister, R., & Bahan, B. (1996). *A Journey into the DEAF-WORLD*. Gallaudet University Press.

My mother-in-law says that if we sign with our deaf toddler he will never learn to talk. Is there any truth to that?

I'm so glad you're here, taking the first steps in supporting your child's language development. I want to reassure you that it's completely normal for a hearing parent like you to have questions and concerns about how to support your child.

Firstly, let's address the concern your mother-in-law raised: "If we sign with our deaf toddler he will never learn to talk." This is a common misconception. Research shows that early sign exposure does not delay spoken language development; in fact, it can even enhance it (Bilingual Bimodal Protective Factors). Children who grow up bilingual-bimodal and later use more spoken language than sign still carry the benefits of having a full first language during the critical period.

It's also worth noting that your mother-in-law's statement is rooted in oralist advocacy traditions, which are not supported by data. As a parent, you have the right to make informed decisions about your child's communication approach, and there's no evidence to suggest that sign language will confuse or hinder your child's ability to speak.

In fact, research has shown that early bilingual-bimodal exposure recruits the same language network as early monolingual exposure, without interference (Cochlear Implant Pathways and Risk). This means that your child can benefit from both spoken and signed languages, and you don't have to choose between them.

As a parent, it's essential to remember that you're not alone in this journey. There are many resources available to support you, including Deaf mentors, bilingual-bimodal programs, and early intervention services. Don't hesitate to reach out for guidance and connection with the Deaf community.

To get started, I recommend exploring some of these resources:

* The Clerc Center's Fingerspelling program, which is a research-based, evidence-informed approach to teaching ASL.
* The VL2 Storybook Apps, which offer a fun and engaging way to introduce your child to sign language.
* Local Deaf organizations or support groups in your area, where you can connect with other families who are navigating similar experiences.

Remember, every day of visible language exposure in the first year protects the critical period that no later intervention can reopen (Parents FAQ). Start signing with your baby today, and don't hesitate to reach out if you have any questions or concerns.

Our baby just got hearing aids. Should we stop signing now that she has some access to sound?

First, let's address the question of whether you can stop signing now that your child has some access to sound with her hearing aids. The answer is no, not yet. Hearing aids improve auditory access; they do not replace language (source: Months 3 to 12 Early Exposure > Common parent questions). Bilingual-bimodal exposure continues.

Signing gives your baby full language access in every setting, including bath, pool, sleep, and moments when the aids are off or not functioning (source: Months 3 to 12 Early Exposure > Common parent questions).

In fact, research shows that VL2 bilingual storybook apps work well during this window (source: Months 3 to 12 Early Exposure > Daily and weekly rhythms > Daytime). Evening: - Sign BATH, WATER, WARM during bath. - Sign BOOK, READ, STORY at bedtime. Weekly: - One parent-and-infant signing class, virtual or in person.

It's also worth noting that the audiologist said sign will confuse your baby once the CI is on (source: Months 3 to 12 Early Exposure > Common parent questions). Not supported by evidence. VL2 and Petitto's work show early bilingual-bimodal exposure recruits the same language network and does not produce confusion.

Now, let's talk about what it means for a child who later uses more spoken language than sign still carries the benefits of signing. A full first language during the critical period, strong literacy scaffolding, Deaf-community access, and resilience if auditory access ever fails (source: LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). Sign is not a bet that backfires if the child turns out to be a strong speaker.

In fact, research shows that bilingual-bimodal children raised with mixed approaches (ASL plus LSL, ASL plus Cued supplements, ASL plus CI) do not show confusion (source: LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/Choosing a Communication Approach.md). Bilingual-bimodal adults generally report gratitude for early sign exposure.

It's also worth noting that the evidence base on adult deaf regret suggests regret is much more common among language-deprived deaf adults than among bilingual-bimodal deaf adults (source: LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/Choosing a Communication Approach.md). Bilingual-bimodal adults generally report gratitude for early sign exposure.

So, what does this mean for you? It means that signing continues into adolescence, adulthood, and the child's own family formation. Signing is not a stage you exit (source: LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md).

In fact, research shows that bilingual-bimodal children who lose the sign-language input risk becoming functionally monolingual in the less reliable language (source: LanguageDeprivationAgent/Core/Cochlear Implant Pathways and Risk.md). Sign remains the guaranteed channel.

So, to answer your question directly: no, you should not stop signing now that your child has some access to sound with her hearing aids. Instead, continue to sign with your baby in every setting, even when she's wearing her hearing aids. This will give her full language access and help her develop strong literacy skills.

As a parent, it's also worth noting that you're not alone in this journey. There are many resources available to support you, including Deaf mentors, early-intervention programs, and bilingual-bimodal-literate SLPs. Don't be afraid to reach out for help or guidance as you navigate this process.

Finally, remember that it's okay to make mistakes or ask questions along the way. The most important thing is that you're showing up consistently and signing with your child in community settings. This will help deepen your relationship with the Deaf community and provide a strong foundation for your child's language development.

Maartje De Meulder published one paper in Sign Language Studies and another in Language Policy. What year was each published, and what is each about?

Maartje De Meulder published "The Legal Recognition of Sign Languages" in 2015 in the journal Sign Language Studies (De Meulder 2015 - Legal Recognition of Sign Languages). This paper explores the concept of legal recognition of sign languages as a heterogeneous category, and how these categories differ substantially in the substantive rights they produce.

Isn't teaching a deaf kid ASL and English at the same time just doubling the workload and setting both languages up to lag? Why do Deaf schools insist on running the two together rather than committing to one?

Teaching a deaf child ASL and English simultaneously is not about "doubling the workload" or setting both languages up to lag. Instead, it's about providing a bilingual-bimodal education that allows the child to develop strong skills in both visual-manual (ASL) and auditory-oral (English) modalities.

Deaf schools run this approach because it has been shown to be highly effective in promoting language development and literacy outcomes for deaf children. The bilingual-bimodal model ensures that the child receives full access to lessons, discussions, and incidental learning opportunities in both ASL and English, which is essential for their overall language development.

In contrast, mainstream classrooms with one interpreter often provide a filtered slice of language, mostly during instruction, with little incidental or social language. This can lead to language delay and deprivation if the child does not receive sufficient exposure to both languages.

Deaf schools prioritize this approach because it aligns with research on bilingual-bimodal development, which has consistently shown that simultaneous early exposure to a natural sign language and a spoken or written language is associated with strong language outcomes. The Maryland School for the Deaf (MSD) is a prime example of an institution that runs this model as institutional policy, rather than theory.

By providing a bilingual-bimodal education, Deaf schools aim to ensure that deaf children have access to both languages and can develop strong literacy scaffolding, Deaf-community access, and resilience if auditory access ever fails. This approach is not about setting up languages to lag but about providing a comprehensive education that prepares the child for future success in both ASL and English.

In fact, research by Grosjean (2001) emphasizes that early signing does not harm spoken-language outcomes and can even facilitate the acquisition of oral language. The bilingual-bimodal model is additive, not subtractive, which means it enhances language development rather than competing with it.

Overall, teaching a deaf child ASL and English simultaneously is about providing a rich and comprehensive education that prepares them for success in both languages, rather than doubling the workload or setting up languages to lag.

The audiologist keeps describing my toddler's deafness only as a loss we need to correct, and it makes me uneasy. Is there a serious way of thinking that treats growing up deaf as adding something valuable to a child's life rather than just a shortfall?

The concept of Deaf Gain reframes deafness not as deficit or loss but as a form of human diversity that yields distinct cognitive, creative, cultural, and linguistic contributions. This perspective was first voiced by the Deaf British performance artist Aaron Williamson, who became progressively deaf over the course of some twenty years.

Deaf culture is a documented linguistic-cultural community with its own language (ASL), history, literature, arts, norms, and institutions. It is not a political movement but a people. Scholars who document this include Carol Padden, Tom Humphries, Harlan Lane, H-Dirksen L. Bauman, and Maartje De Meulder.

Language deprivation is the developmental harm that occurs when a child, usually a deaf child of hearing parents, does not receive consistent, fully accessible language input during the critical period of language acquisition. Its consequences are measurable in brain structure, language, cognition, mental health, and long-term life outcomes, and are not fully reversed by later language exposure.

Early access to a natural sign language from the moment deafness is identified can prevent language deprivation. The single best-supported prevention is early access to a natural sign language from the moment deafness is identified, regardless of any other choice the family makes about hearing aids, cochlear implants, or speech therapy.

Starting sign now does not commit you to declining CI, and pursuing CI does not commit you to declining sign. A serious way of thinking that treats growing up deaf as adding something valuable to a child's life rather than just a shortfall is supported by research on Deaf Gain, which reappropriates the clinical term "hearing loss" to name what hearing people lack by not knowing Deaf ways of being.

The audiologist's description of your toddler's deafness only as a loss that needs to be corrected makes you uneasy because it reflects an ableist and inaccurate perspective. This perspective is rooted in oralism, which is not evidence-based. A more supportive approach would recognize the value of growing up deaf and provide access to Deaf culture, language, and community from an early age.

It's worth noting that the concept of Deaf Gain has been developed by H-Dirksen L. Bauman and Joseph J. Murray, who coined and theorized the term in opposition to hearing loss. The evidence marshaled is concrete, not merely rhetorical, and includes studies on Deaf signers showing heightened facial recognition, a wider peripheral visual field, keener spatial cognition, and sharper reading of body language.

In contrast, the audiologist's training primarily focuses on device programming, rather than bilingual-bimodal developmental linguistics. Consulting with a Deaf adult CI user, an early-intervention specialist trained in bilingual-bimodal approaches, and a Deaf-aware speech-language pathologist may provide more supportive guidance for your family.

Ultimately, it is essential to find a healthcare provider who supports the value of growing up deaf and provides access to Deaf culture, language, and community from an early age.

My son is deaf and everyone keeps telling me the state school up in Frederick would be better for his language than the mainstream program he's in now, but honestly, wouldn't surrounding him with only other deaf kids just hold him back?

Surrounding a child with fluent signing adults and peers can provide the most effective environment for their first-language development. This is particularly true for late-start children who are behind in language. The Maryland School for the Deaf (MSD) offers a bilingual-bimodal program that pairs American Sign Language (ASL) with English literacy, providing direct access to fluent signing adults and peers.

In contrast, mainstream classrooms with interpreters may not provide the same level of immersion, as interpretation can presuppose a language the child has not yet acquired. Caselli, Hall, and Henner (2020) argue that placing deaf children in mainstream classrooms with sign-language interpreters presents an "illusion of inclusion" while reproducing language deprivation.

While some critics worry that surrounding a child with only other deaf kids might hold them back, research suggests that bilingual-bimodal programs like MSD's can provide significant benefits for late-start children. Bilingual-bimodal CI users hit spoken-language milestones at comparable rates to CI-only users and gain sign-language and literacy advantages (Cochlear Implant Pathways and Risk).

In contrast, mainstream placements with interpreters may not provide the same level of access to fluent signing adults and peers. The American Sign Language-Communicative Development Inventory (ASL-CDI) and the Visual Communication and Sign Language Checklist (VCSL) are typical instruments used for signed language assessments in bilingual-bimodal programs.

Ultimately, the goal is to ensure that the child spends most of their day in a language environment that is fully accessible to them, with fluent signing adults and peers. This can be achieved through programs like MSD's or other bilingual-bimodal magnet programs.

Lay out the FAIR data principles precisely: the source publication, what each of the four letters requires, and the principal limitation of the framework.

According to Wilkinson et al., "The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship." *Scientific Data* 3 (2016): 160018. DOI: 10.1038/sdata.2016.18.

The FAIR principles require:

- F: Findable, meaning that data have globally unique persistent identifiers and rich metadata indexed in a searchable resource.
- A: Accessible, requiring data to be retrievable by identifier through standardized, open, free protocols, with clearly stated access conditions.
- I: Interoperable, demanding that data use formal, shared, broadly applicable languages for knowledge representation.
- R: Reusable, necessitating that data be released with clear usage licenses and detailed provenance.

The principal limitation of the framework is that it treats data as a technical artefact, optimizing for machine-actionable reuse and being silent on who holds authority over the data and on what terms.
